name: Lena Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead the evening appointment team at a medical contact centre, answering calls and chats when a patient needs a scan moved or a referral checked. My two-year college diploma is in health administration, and I am among the agents people come to when a slot, referral and transport booking do not agree. The evening allowance makes my pay higher than the usual agent rate. I use an approved AI note summary now and then, after another shift has tried it, but I check the actual referral and clinic diary before I move a patient.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that shift fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Malik works a daytime bus-depot rota, and our grown children have their own homes. We rent, have about nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other centres and clinics reachable from here. The evening allowance has helped us build that reserve, though Malik’s hours can change. We have not verified what income would cover us if I eventually stopped working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team a quicker appointment note is useful only if it names the same clinic as the referral. Last week the summary called a heart scan a routine check, so I opened the actual letter before moving the slot. The patient had arranged transport for a particular entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the evening desk stays busy if AI merely saves a little writing. Nine months saved and many nearby centres make this a comfortable position for now. I still want the higher evening rate, but I do not need to chase every new program before the clinic has tested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid evening calls and compare approved summaries with referral letters and clinic diaries. Once a month Malik and I would check actual rent, wages and transport bills against our existing reserve. I would not call that adding new savings; it tells us whether nine months is still the right number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work. A patient still needs the right scan at the right entrance. A little faster writing is welcome if the letter remains the authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a public tool to read referrals faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not send referral letters to an outside AI service. The approved summary is inside the centre, and I can open the original while I am on my paid shift. I would not ask a patient to trust a shortcut we cannot check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does checking the reserve mean you plan to save more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The monthly comparison is a measure, not a contribution. If rent rises, nine months might become eight. Malik and I would then discuss the real budget rather than call the old figure a guarantee.

Compare actual rent, wages, transport bills and existing savings with Malik monthly

say: I would say **routine bookings** may move to AI while tangled referrals still need checking.
I would ask for **written paid hours** and a supervised dummy-case test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can book an ordinary follow-up quickly, but a patient with two referrals can still be sent to the wrong scanner. I would ask for the written paid evening rota and a supervised test of the new AI slot matcher on closed, invented appointment cases. The whole point is to see whether it puts the transport booking at the right entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer routine booking calls could mean fewer evening hours for me. My lead skill helps with tangled referrals, but the allowance is paid for hours, not for being trusted. Nine months saved and nearby clinics give us options, not the same Friday wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre approves the test and pays the time, I would learn the new AI slot matcher on twenty dummy referral-and-transport pairs, checking its result against the clinic diary. I would keep answering live patient calls on my paid rota and ask for written weekly evening hours. If those paid hours actually fall, I would compare posted paid clinic-reception jobs by written weekly wages and hours covering rent, utilities and fares after travel before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a shorter evening week, though I can look nearby. I am willing to learn a tool after a proper test. I do not want an error in a patient’s journey to be called efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use real patient letters to test the matcher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not use actual patient letters in the test unless the centre approved their use and removed identifying details. Dummy cases are enough for the first twenty. If the test is not approved or paid, I would keep using the existing system on my normal paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any job with the word reception make you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a reception job really handles referrals or just points to a kiosk, but that is an enquiry, not a secret rule against applying. I would need the posted paid opening and written full-week wage and hours after fares before accepting. I would leave my evening rota only after a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Malik full AGI by 2028 could organise appointment screens and answer patients before a new evening rota is printed. Robots helping with hands-on clinic work around 2031 come later; the calls and bookings are exposed first. I would ask the centre for actual dates of paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of our routine evening calls could disappear, perhaps enough to cut my own allowance sharply. Nine months saved would let us search without a panic sale, but Malik’s variable bus-depot hours cannot be our only rent plan. There are many clinics, yet I need a posted paid opening rather than a building with a reception sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week in 2026 I would compare our last eight full-week payslips with rent, utilities and transport costs. If most of my paid evening hours end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid clinic desks only if written weekly wages and hours cover those costs after travel and the first bus fits the shift. I would keep any remaining paid calls until a suitable offer is signed, and review the use of our existing savings with Malik after no more than six search weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a sharp cut to hours, though nine months saved and many clinics let us reject a thin rota. A clinic sign on a building is not a paid shift. I want the written week before I tell Malik we are all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you draw on savings before paid hours actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six weeks is a point to review bills and actual offers with Malik, not a limit on the entire search or new saving. We would touch the existing nine-month reserve only if most paid evening hours actually end. I would not assume our children can replace the allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would referral-correction authority be an application condition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a clinic desk can correct a wrong referral and what hours it is staffed. I would weigh that answer, but I would not turn an unanswered question into an automatic refusal to apply. Written weekly wages and hours, fares, a fitting first bus and a signed offer decide whether I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team five years lets us show which appointment errors actually stranded a patient at the wrong entrance. Thinking AGI could run scheduling by 2031; robots moving equipment at clinics may follow around 2034. We should ask the manager for paid time to check the new schedule against real, permitted closed cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can still lead a team that fixes failed referrals, but I do not know whether the evening allowance will survive. Nine months saved and many clinics let me look carefully. I would rather take a paid trial at an outpatient reception than buy a qualification that no posted role asks for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would keep a permitted list of fifteen corrected appointment errors during paid calls, without patient names. If the clinic posts a paid outpatient-reception opening with a two-day paid trial, I would try it only if the written trial wages and hours are clear, I lose no paid evening calls, and the first bus fits; I would not pay a trial fee. I would accept a full role only if written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after travel and a suitable offer is signed; if no opening appears or evening hours fall around 2031, I would check other posted paid clinics by the same full-week test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cut to my paid evening hours, but five years gives me time to test a real desk. A paid trial would show whether the clinic needs my referral skill. It would not by itself replace a full week of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you surrender an evening shift to try the reception desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not swap a paid evening call for a trial shift. The trial must fit around my current paid rota and have written paid hours and wages of its own. I would also check the first bus before promising to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the fifteen-error list contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen errors would come from cases the centre permits us to study, with names removed, and I would record them while paid. I would ask the manager to compare the original referral with the corrected slot. That is current lead work, not a new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Malik a decade lets us check real household wages and rent each year before we talk about fewer evenings at work. Thinking AGI may change appointment calls by 2036, while robots in clinics would be later, around 2039. I would keep the lead rota while it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might want more evenings at home in ten years, but I cannot name an income that replaces my wage yet. Nine months saved is generous search room, not a retirement payment. Malik’s bus-depot hours may change too, so we need actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year Malik and I would compare actual wages, rent, utilities, travel and any verified retirement income. I would keep paid appointment calls and coach a newer agent on checking referral and transport details during paid shifts. If evening hours fall after 2036 and my wage remains needed, I would seek posted paid clinic desks with written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare, leaving only on a suitable signed offer with a bus that runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the time to plan and the nearby clinics, with some concern about unverified future income. We can enjoy a quiet evening without declaring a retirement date today. I want the numbers before a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade make you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not choose a retirement date from the AGI card. We would first need documented income and the real household bills. If wages are still needed, I keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would coaching a newer agent be an extra evening class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coaching is already part of my paid lead work, and I would not turn it into an unpaid evening class. If paid calls shrink, I would compare full weekly wages and hours at clinics after fare. I would keep the current paid rota until a suitable new offer is signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most evening appointment hours could end before I know which clinics have a full paid week. Nine months saved gives Malik and me a search, not a replacement allowance. Written shift dates and posted paid reception roles with full weekly wages and hours would help us choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A patient can arrive at the right hospital and still miss a scan by using the wrong entrance. Someone has to check the referral, the diary and the transport booking together.

headlineQuote: A patient can arrive at the right hospital and still miss a scan by using the wrong entrance.
portrait: At **58**, Lena leads medical appointments with a health-administration diploma and strong referral knowledge.
She and Malik rent with **nine months saved**; her evening allowance lifts pay, and many clinics are nearby.
She uses **approved AI occasionally**, then checks referrals, diaries and transport details.
She would try a **paid clinic trial** without losing current paid evening calls.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end most paid evening hours before a full-week clinic role appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written paid dates** and posted paid reception roles with complete weekly wages and hours.
